shared.title: The Power of Default Options
shared.text:
When people face a choice, they often stick with whatever option has been selected for them in advance. Behavioral economists call this preselected choice a "default," and research shows that defaults can strongly shape decisions, even when changing them is easy and free.

One well-known example comes from retirement savings. At many companies, employees once had to actively sign up for a savings plan, and a large share never did. When some employers changed the rule so that workers were enrolled automatically unless they chose to leave the plan, participation rose dramatically. The workers' options had not changed at all; only the starting point had.

Researchers offer several explanations for this pattern. First, changing a default requires effort, and people tend to postpone tasks that seem complicated. Second, many people interpret the default as a recommendation, assuming that whoever designed the system chose the sensible option. Finally, people often feel a loss more strongly than an equal gain, so giving up the default can feel like losing something. Because defaults are so powerful, critics argue that the people who design them carry a real responsibility. A poorly chosen default can quietly lead thousands of people toward decisions that do not serve their interests.

shared.title: How bats use echolocation
shared.text:
OK, so today we're looking at how bats find their way in the dark. Many bats, especially the ones that hunt insects, are active at night. So the question is: how do you catch a tiny moth in total darkness? The answer is echolocation.

Here's how it works. A bat produces a series of very high-pitched calls, and most of them are too high for humans to hear. These sounds travel outward, hit objects, and bounce back as echoes. The bat's large, sensitive ears pick up those echoes, and its brain uses them to build a kind of sound picture of its surroundings. By sensing how long an echo takes to return, the bat can tell how far away something is. And small differences between the echoes reaching its left and right ears help it figure out direction.

Now, what's really clever is how the calls change during a hunt. When a bat is just searching, it calls fairly slowly, maybe ten times a second. But once it detects an insect, it speeds up. Right before the catch, some bats call more than a hundred and fifty times a second. Researchers call this the "feeding buzz." Faster calls mean more frequent updates, so the bat can keep track of an insect that's twisting and turning.

But the insects haven't just accepted this. Some moths have evolved ears that can detect bat calls, and when they hear one, they dive or fly in unpredictable loops. So it's kind of an evolutionary arms race, with each side adapting to the other.
